name: Piotroski value
summary: Cheap on price to book, with a strong 9-point financial-health score.
how_to_read: Two filters must both pass: price to book in the cheapest 30% of the universe, and a Piotroski F-score of at least 8 out of 9. The F-score adds up nine pass/fail tests comparing the latest fiscal year with the one before: profitability (ROA, operating cash flow, change in ROA, cash flow above net income), funding (less leverage, a better current ratio, no new shares) and efficiency (a better gross margin and asset turnover). Piotroski applied it to the cheapest fifth of stocks by book-to-market. Glint uses the cheapest 30% by P/B to get a workable list: many companies are missing one of the nine inputs, so the cheapest fifth leaves very few. Glint shows the list. It doesn't test or claim any returns.
misses: The years ahead: a high score says the latest year improved on the one before, and nothing about the years ahead.
Companies whose book value understates the business (brands, software, buybacks that shrank equity).
Any company with one of the nine inputs missing from its filings, because the score is then missing.
Banks and insurers: the score isn't meaningful for them, so they never pass.
source: Piotroski, 'Value Investing: The Use of Historical Financial Statement Information to Separate Winners from Losers', Journal of Accounting Research (2000)
